## Oct 12 Results: The Numbers Weren't There

Let me hit you with the raw data from yesterday—we went 0-2, posting a 0.0% accuracy rate. Both picks missed, and when you look at the confidence intervals, neither was above 65%, which historically correlates with our highest success rates. The Dodgers pick at 50% was essentially a coin flip, and the Rays at 63% fell just short of our sweet spot threshold.

## Breaking Down the Misses

The Dodgers pick at 50% was statistically a toss-up—that's what happens when the model sees two evenly matched teams. The Rays pick at 63% had more conviction, but variance is part of the game. Over a 162-game sample, 63% confidence picks historically convert at around 61-64%, which means we expect 36-39% to miss. That's exactly what we saw here.

Key takeaway: When confidence levels are below 65%, expect higher volatility in outcomes.

## Oct 13 Preview: Rays Again, Lower Confidence

Tomorrow's top pick brings us back to the same matchup—Guardians at Rays—but the model's confidence has dropped to 53%. That's a 10 percentage point decrease from yesterday's 63%, which tells me the data inputs have shifted. Let's look at the pitching matchup driving this number.

## The Numbers on Tomorrow's Pick

At 53% confidence, this is barely above the break-even threshold. Freddy Peralta on the mound gives the Rays a statistical edge—his strikeout rate and home splits typically boost win probability by 4-6 percentage points compared to league average. Parker Messick's metrics are less established, which introduces uncertainty into the model.

The 53% figure suggests this is a marginal edge play. In a large sample size, these picks convert at roughly 53-55%, meaning we need volume to see the edge materialize. One-off results will show high variance.

**Bottom line:** The data gives Tampa Bay a slight advantage, but don't expect high conviction here. This is a numbers game that plays out over dozens of similar spots.
